scenes.text: Your phone unlocks with your face, your gallery finds every picture of your dog, and cars can spot pedestrians. [1] All of this is computer vision. [2] Let's understand how AI sees images.

Computer vision is the field of AI that understands images and videos. [1] To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers, one for each pixel's colour. [2] The model finds edges and shapes, [3] then objects, [4] and finally, what's happening in the scene.

data.definition: AI that understands images and video, starting from a grid of pixel numbers.

scenes.text: Computer vision has four classic tasks. [1] Classification, what's in this image? A cat. [2] Detection, where are the objects? It draws a box around each one. [3] Segmentation, which exact pixels belong to each object. [4] And tracking, following objects across video frames.

Inside, it works in layers, just like we saw in episode one. [1] It starts with raw pixels. [2] Early layers find edges. [3] Middle layers combine them into shapes. [4] And later layers recognise whole objects.

There are two main designs. [1] Convolutional networks slide small filters across the image, looking at nearby pixels, and they're great at local patterns. [2] Vision transformers cut the image into patches, and use attention, from episode 27, to relate every patch to every other.
And it's everywhere. [1] Face unlock, and photo search on your phone. [2] Cameras that read number plates at toll plazas. [3] And factories that spot defects on production lines.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think computer vision sees the world just like we do. [2] It can be fooled by things humans ignore, like odd lighting, unusual angles, or tiny changes to pixels. That's why safety critical systems use multiple checks.

data.myth: Computer vision sees the world just like we do.
data.fact: It can be fooled by odd lighting, angles or tiny pixel changes, so critical systems double-check.
